skill.name: env-handler
skill.description: Manage environment variable templates and local secret files with clear project conventions.
skill.summary: Guides safe separation of committed .env templates from local secret overrides.
skill.author: AayushBaniya2006

security_audit.summary: The skill is documentation-only and I found no prompt injection, exfiltration intent, or executable command behavior. The main confirmed risk is legitimate but sensitive environment-file handling around .env and .env.local, which requires strong guardrails before publication.

remediation.issue: The skill operates near .env.local, which is intended to contain real secrets.
remediation.suggestion: Add an explicit rule to never read, print, summarize, or copy existing .env.local values. Only ask users to enter secret values locally.

remediation.issue: The reference uses realistic credential-shaped examples for local secrets.
remediation.suggestion: Replace sample database URLs and secret hashes with clearly fake placeholders that cannot be mistaken for usable credentials.

remediation.issue: Environment file edits can accidentally commit sensitive values.
remediation.suggestion: Require a final check that committed .env entries for sensitive variables are empty before any commit or deployment step.

content.value_statement: Environment variables often mix public defaults with private secrets. This skill guides Claude, Codex, and Claude Code to keep templates separate from local secrets.
actual_capabilities: Defines .env as the committed template for defaults and empty secret placeholders.
Defines .env.local as the ignored file for real local secrets and overrides.
Provides steps for adding a new sensitive variable without placing the value in .env.
Provides steps for adding public or non-sensitive configuration values.
Documents server-side and client-side environment variable naming conventions.
Includes a checklist for reviewing environment variable changes.
limitations: Does not rotate leaked secrets or manage cloud provider accounts.
Does not validate whether environment values are correct at runtime.
Requires user review before editing real project environment files.
Focuses on Next.js and Vercel-style environment conventions.

use_cases.title: Add a Secret Safely
use_cases.description: Add a new API token placeholder to the project template while keeping the actual value in a local ignored file.

use_cases.title: Standardize Deployment Variables
use_cases.description: Review which variables belong in committed templates, local overrides, and hosted deployment settings.

use_cases.title: Review Configuration Changes
use_cases.description: Check an environment variable change for secret exposure before code review or release.

prompt_templates.title: Add a New Secret
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner task for one sensitive variable.
prompt_templates.prompt: Add a placeholder for a new sensitive variable named PAYMENT_API_KEY. Keep the real value out of committed files and tell me where to enter it locally.

prompt_templates.title: Add a Public Setting
prompt_templates.scenario: Basic task for a non-sensitive client setting.
prompt_templates.prompt: Add a public application URL setting for local development. Use the project environment conventions from this skill.

prompt_templates.title: Audit Existing Variables
prompt_templates.scenario: Intermediate review of environment file structure.
prompt_templates.prompt: Review the current environment variable setup. Identify which entries should be templates, local secrets, public values, or deployment settings.

prompt_templates.title: Prepare Deployment Checklist
prompt_templates.scenario: Advanced release preparation across local and hosted environments.
prompt_templates.prompt: Prepare a release checklist for environment variables before deployment. Include template placeholders, local secrets, hosted variables, and final safety checks.

output_examples.input: Add a sensitive token for a new image generation provider.
output_examples.output: The assistant adds an empty template entry, then asks the user to place the real token in the local ignored secrets file.

output_examples.input: Review environment variables before deploying to Vercel.
output_examples.output: The assistant separates public defaults, empty secret placeholders, and hosted production variables, then lists any missing setup steps.

output_examples.input: Check whether a new variable is safe to commit.
output_examples.output: The assistant explains whether the value is public or sensitive and recommends an empty placeholder when the value must remain private.

best_practices: Keep committed template files free of real secret values.
Ask users to enter secrets locally instead of sending them through chat.
Review environment file changes before committing or deploying.
anti_patterns: Do not place live API keys, tokens, or passwords in committed environment files.
Do not ask users to paste secret values into the conversation.
Do not create duplicate environment templates when the project standard uses .env.

faq.question: Does this skill manage real secret values?
faq.answer: No. It guides where secrets should live, but users should enter real values locally.

faq.question: Can it create a .env.example file?
faq.answer: No. The documented convention forbids .env.example and uses .env as the template.

faq.question: Is it suitable for public client variables?
faq.answer: Yes. It includes guidance for public variables that use the NEXT_PUBLIC prefix.

faq.question: Does it support Vercel deployment settings?
faq.answer: Yes. It reminds users to configure production variables in Vercel project settings.

faq.question: Will it detect leaked credentials automatically?
faq.answer: No. It provides process guidance, but separate secret scanning is still needed.

faq.question: Which assistants can use this skill?
faq.answer: The report lists support for Claude, Codex, and Claude Code.
